feedback: If a learner predicted the hard shell was safe, use the fizzing to surface and name the 'hard things are safe from acid' intuition.
If a learner concludes the ocean is 'turning into acid', correct conservatively: seawater remains slightly alkaline; it is becoming less alkaline (lower pH), which is enough to reduce carbonate ions.

If a learner treats vinegar and seawater as equivalent, restate the caveat: the ocean is far weaker and slower, stays slightly alkaline, and mainly works by lowering carbonate ions so skeletons are harder to build and maintain. It shares the acid–carbonate chemistry but does not visibly fizz like vinegar.
activities.intendedInsight: Hard calcium-carbonate structures are not safe from acids; a mildly more acidic ocean is enough to reduce carbonate availability and attack skeletons over time.
learnerActions: Before observing, write a prediction with a reason: could a weak acid damage something as hard as a seashell or coral skeleton? Most people expect 'no, it's too hard'.

Observe a clean shell or a piece of natural chalk or limestone (calcium carbonate) placed in vinegar; note the immediate fizzing (carbon dioxide gas being released) as the surface is attacked and slowly dissolves. Note: many blackboard chalks are calcium sulfate and will not fizz, so check the material first.
Explain the link to ocean acidification: CO2 makes seawater more acidic, attacking the same calcium carbonate that corals and shellfish build.

State the important caveat in your own words: vinegar is far stronger than seawater, so the ocean effect is much slower and gentler. The shared chemistry is that acid reacts with carbonate, but in the ocean this mainly lowers the number of carbonate ions, making skeletons harder to build and easier to wear away, rather than visibly fizzing them away. Seawater stays slightly alkaline and becomes LESS alkaline, not an actual acid.
activities.title: Does acid attack something hard? Predict–Observe–Explain

feedback: If a learner claims shading or restoration can save reefs alone, ask them to trace acidification's cause: lowering water temperature does not remove the extra dissolved CO2, so it cannot reverse the CO2-driven fall in seawater pH.
If a learner cannot name what links warming and acidification, return to the shared root: fossil-fuel CO2 both traps heat and dissolves into seawater.
Credit arguments that explicitly pair an intervention with the cause it addresses and acknowledge trade-offs and uncertainty.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating responses requires matching each intervention to the mechanism it affects; because acidification only eases with reduced CO2, local-only measures are insufficient on their own.
learnerActions: Interview (in role-play or with a knowledgeable persona) a marine biologist who has surveyed a bleaching event; ask what they saw and why some reefs recover while others do not.
Pose the evaluation questions: is restoration worth it? Should effort go to cutting emissions or to engineering heat-tolerant coral? What has already been lost?
Argue, using the two-mechanism model, why local fixes such as shade, cooling, or restoration help bleaching but cannot solve acidification.
State which interventions target which cause, and why reducing CO2 is the only lever that addresses both.
activities.title: Interview a reef scientist: trade-offs and evaluation

feedback: If a learner misorders the chain, have them check that each step is caused by the one before (CO2 before carbonic acid, lower pH before fewer carbonate ions).
If a learner miscategorises a symptom, ask whether temperature or CO2 produced it.
If a learner matches cooling to acidification, point out that cooling does not remove the extra dissolved CO2, so it cannot reverse acidification.
activities.intendedInsight: The two threats have distinct causal chains and distinct fixes; placing each step and symptom in the right chain confirms the learner can keep them separate while recognising the shared CO2 root.
learnerActions: Sequence the acidification chain in order: CO2 → carbonic acid → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → weak/dissolving skeleton.
Categorise a mix of symptoms and causes as either bleaching (thermal) or acidification (chemical).
Match each intervention to the cause it addresses (e.g. shading/cooling → bleaching only; cutting emissions → both).
Estimate how much of emitted CO2 the ocean absorbs (~25–30%) and connect that to why ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era.
activities.title: Sort and sequence: consolidate the two chains
